query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, dense anti-oxidation coating (e.g., an alumina-based or similar oxide coating) to as‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures without degrading its room-temperature ductility or elevated-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (strain rates 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1), but with poor inherent oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, adherent, and dense anti-oxidation coating (for example, an alumina-based coating applied via thermal spraying or chemical vapor deposition) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Expose coated samples to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (around 1000 °C in air) for extended periods (e.g., 100 hours) while subjecting them to strain rates similar to the baseline tests (10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1) to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, stable oxide scale at the surface, which acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The coating prevents oxygen ingress by forming a protective oxide layer that is chemically and thermally stable at high temperatures, thereby preserving the underlying alloy’s microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit significantly improved oxygen resistance (reduced oxidation weight gain and surface degradation) at high temperature while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility and elevated-temperature yield strength to the uncoated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr shows poor oxygen resistance, limiting its practical high-temperature use despite useful mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under steady-state high-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere; its performance under cyclic thermal shocks or extreme mechanical fatigue conditions remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the long-term adhesion and stability of the coating under cyclic thermal loading and severe mechanical deformation, which could affect both oxidation protection and mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. Apply the chosen anti-oxidation coating to one set while leaving the other set uncoated. Expose both sets to 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. Perform tensile tests (at room temperature for ductility and at 1000 °C for yield strength at strain rates between 10^−4 and 10^−2 s^−1) before and after exposure. Compare oxidation weight gains, microstructural integrity (via SEM/XRD), and mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain and surface morphology changes (SEM, XRD)
Elevated-temperature yield strength (MPa) at controlled strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples exhibit oxidation behavior (weight gain, surface degradation) similar to the uncoated samples, or if there is a significant (>10%) reduction in tensile ductility or yield strength after coating and exposure relative to the baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
